new_statements.quote: Sa Surigaonon-Cantilan karaniwang binibigkas nang may diin ang mga salitang higit sa isang pantig. [...] Tuldik na paiwa (ˋ) ang ginagamit sa mga salitang binibigkas nang malumi, pahilis (ˋ) kung ang bigkas ng salita ay mabilis at pakupya naman (ˆ) kung ito'y binibigkas nang maragsa. Inilalagay ang mga tuldik na ito sa itaas ng huling patinig ng salita. [...] Ang Talahanayan 6 ay nagpapakita ng mga salitang Cantilangnun na magkapareho ang baybay ngunit magkaiba ang kanilang kahulugan dahil sa diin ng pagkabigkas nito. Tulad na lamang ng salitang amo, mayroon itong apat na kahulugan bunga ng pagkakaiba ng diin nito.
new_statements.translation: In Surigaonon-Cantilan, words of more than one syllable are normally pronounced with a stress. [...] The grave mark (ˋ) is used for words pronounced malumi [penultimate stress + final glottal stop], the acute when the word's pronunciation is mabilis [final stress], and the circumflex (ˆ) when it is pronounced maragsa [final stress + final glottal stop]. These marks are placed above the final vowel of the word. [...] Table 6 shows Cantilangnun words that are spelled the same but differ in meaning because of the stress with which they are pronounced. For instance the word amo has four meanings resulting from differences in its stress. [Table 6, p. 69: a.mo 'landlord' (malumay), a.mò 'ours' (malumi), amó 'really' (mabilis), amô 'monkey' (maragsa); ba.jad 'payment' vs bajád 'paid'; sa.jaw 'dance' vs sajáw 'a kind of bird'; ja.un 'there is' vs jaún 'that'; wayá 'left' vs wayâ 'none'.]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Surigaonon has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this article supplies the first placement statement: contrastive (lexical) stress on the penult or the final syllable, illustrated with minimal pairs. Citation correction: the listed entry 'Samarca, [given name not verified]' is Annie Y. Samarca with co-author Mary Ann S. Sandoval, Vol. 20 (Special Edition) 2022, pp. 59-73. The listed open_url (research.buksu.edu.ph) no longer resolves; the journal has moved to apjsbs.buksu.edu.ph, where the article is id 32 (PDF galley download/32/42).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is phonemic in Surigaonon-Cantilan: every polysyllabic word carries one stress, on either the penultimate syllable (the Filipino-school types malumay and malumi) or the final syllable (mabilis and maragsa), the presence of a final glottal stop cross-cutting the two placements to give the four-way classification; placement is not predictable and minimal pairs (a.mo / amó / a.mò / amô) differ by stress alone. No general default position is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. The description covers the Cantilan variety (Surigaonon-Cantilan, 'Cantilangnun') spoken in the towns of Carrascal, Cantilan, Madrid, Carmen and Lanuza, Surigao del Sur; the authors mark stress with the Filipino tuldik conventions rather than IPA.
new_statements.identity_note: Samarca and Sandoval 2022 describe Surigaonon-Cantilan (Cantilangnun), the Cantilan-area variety of Surigao del Sur (Carrascal, Cantilan, Madrid, Carmen, Lanuza); Glottolog subsumes Cantilangnon under Surigaonon [sgd]. Atos et al. 2015 is a sketch of 'Hinigakit' (Hinagakit), which Glottolog equates with Surigaonon [sgd]. Dumanig 2015 (context only) describes Surigaonon of Surigao (del Norte).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every quoted sentence and the locators (pp.216, 218, 50; pdf = book + 24) were confirmed verbatim on the page images we hold of Zorc 1977. (2) Deciding source: a 1977 comparative-historical survey of Bisayan (PL C-44) whose accent statements are pan-Bisayan but explicitly include Sur (accent pair lútuq : lutúq cited for Sur, p.218; Sur not among the varieties that lost accent, 8.10.1). (3) Web/bibliographic search (CiNii, Crossref, Glottolog, UPD Linguistics site; general search engines unreachable) found one open Surigaonon-specific phonology article, Dumanig 2015, downloaded and read: sec. 4.3 p.6 states stress placement 'changes the meaning of the word' and tabulates six penult-vs-final minimal pairs, independently confirming lexical/word for Surigaonon proper; it is silent on the CVC-penult sub-rule and on length, so the secondary/weight fields continue to rest on Zorc alon

sources.quote: 'The stress in Surigaonon is indicated by an apostrophe (') where the stressed syllable is always given more emphasis by increasing the pitch and loudness. In some cases, the change of stressed syllable also changes the meaning of the word.' Table 6 lists 'Penultimate Stressed Words' vs 'Final Stressed Words' minimal pairs: buyag 'separate (adj.)' : buyag 'to separate'; waya? 'none' : waya 'left'; amo 'master' : amo? 'monkey'; buhi? 'to free' : buhi? 'alive'; uban 'white hair' : uban 'accompany'; tuyo? 'spill' : tuyo 'three'. 'there are words in the Surigaonon language that are spelled similar
